summary: Describes a URN namespace for persistent resources published by the International Press Telecommunications Council (IPTC), such as XML schemas, DTDs, stylesheets, and other document formats.

plainLanguage.summary: It gives permanent names to the news industry's shared documents, like library call numbers that never change even if the book moves shelves.

questions: how do uniform resource names work
subtitle: Assigning persistent identifiers to news industry standards and resources.

tldr.problem: The International Press Telecommunications Council (IPTC) publishes various XML schemas, DTDs, stylesheets, and other resources in support of news industry standards. These resources needed a way to be identified with globally unique, persistent, and location-independent names.
tldr.mechanism: IPTC registered a URN (Uniform Resource Name) namespace called 'iptc' following RFC 3406. The namespace uses a hierarchical structure with three branches: 'std' for standards resources, 'std-draft' for draft standards resources, and 'workdoc' for other IPTC work documents. Each URN in the structure includes identifiers for the standard name, version, resource group (spec, doc, or xmlns), resource name, and resource version.
tldr.outcome: IPTC resources now have permanent, unambiguous identifiers that remain valid even if the location of the resource changes, enabling reliable citation and reference in protocols and documents worldwide.

today: RFC 3937 is an Informational RFC that formally registers the IPTC URN namespace with IANA. It enables IPTC to assign permanent identifiers to news industry standards and resources.

sections.title: About IPTC and URN Namespaces
sections.content:
The International Press Telecommunications Council (IPTC) is a nonprofit consortium of the world's major news agencies and news industry vendors established in 1965. IPTC develops and maintains technical standards used by virtually every major news organization in the world. Since the 1990s, IPTC's standardization work has been based on open standards including SGML, XML, MIME, and Unicode.

As these standards require identification of resources, IPTC sought a technology for globally unique, persistent, and location-independent identifiers. They chose to implement URNs (Uniform Resource Names) as described in RFC 2141. Unlike URLs, which specify where something is located, URNs provide permanent names that remain valid even if the resource moves. This RFC describes the formal URN namespace IPTC registered with IANA.
sections.plainLanguage: The news industry has standards, schemas, and documents. They needed names that last forever, no matter where the files move.

sections.title: The URN Namespace Structure
sections.content:
The IPTC URN namespace has three main branches, each serving a different purpose. The std branch is for resources that specify or explain IPTC standards. A URN in this branch has the structure urn:iptc:std:{std-name}:{std-version}:{res-group}{:res-name}?{:res-version}?, where std-name uniquely identifies a standard (like NewsML), std-version identifies which version of the standard (with 'current' pointing to the latest), res-group specifies whether it is a spec resource, documentation, or an XML namespace declaration, and the optional res-name and res-version fields identify a specific resource file.

The std-draft branch uses an identical structure but for resources that have not yet been formally approved by the IPTC Standards body. The workdoc branch is for other IPTC resources not directly related to standards. It uses the structure urn:iptc:workdoc:{group-id}:{doc-id}:{doc-version}{:doc-descr}?, where fields identify the working group, the specific document, its version, and an optional description.
sections.plainLanguage: URNs are organized into groups: finished standards get one type of name, draft standards get another, and other work gets a third. Each name includes what the resource is for, which standard it belongs to, and which version.

sections.title: URN Examples
sections.content:
The RFC provides concrete examples. urn:iptc:std:NewsML:1.1:spec:DTD:1 identifies DTD version 1 for specifying the NewsML standard version 1.1. urn:iptc:std-draft:NITF:3.5:spec:xml-schema:2 identifies the second draft XML Schema for the NITF standard version 3.5. urn:iptc:std:SportsML:1.0:xmlns is a URN for an XML namespace declaration for SportsML version 1.0 (it needs no resource name or version since XML namespaces are not physical files).

For supporting documentation, urn:iptc:std:NewsML:1.1:doc:news-agency-guidelines:1.2 identifies version 1.2 of a supporting document named 'news-agency-guidelines' for NewsML 1.1. For non-standards work, urn:iptc:workdoc:NMA:0315:1:srs-terms identifies version 1 of a work document from the News Metadata Working Party (NMA) related to the Subject Reference System terms.
sections.plainLanguage: An example URN might be the permanent name for 'NewsML version 1.1 specification DTD version 1'. Another might be 'NITF version 3.5 draft schema version 2'. Each piece of the name tells what and when.

sections.title: Registration and Management
sections.content:
IPTC registered this namespace with IANA following the formal procedure defined in RFC 3406. The registration version of this initial entry is 1, dated November 11, 2003. Unique identifiers are enforced by the Managing Director of IPTC, who assigns URNs to all resources within this namespace.

IPTC commits to maintaining the accessibility and persistence of all resources identified by an IPTC URN. Assignment of URNs is limited to IPTC and its authorized agents. IPTC will develop appropriate mechanisms to map assigned URNs to URLs, enabling web-based resolution. Rules for lexical equivalence follow RFC 2141 with no special considerations.
sections.plainLanguage: One person at IPTC assigns the names. IPTC promises to keep the resources available forever and will provide a way to look up where each resource actually lives on the web.

references.text: Coates, A., Allen, D. and D. Rivers-Moore, "URN Namespace for NewsML Resources", RFC 3085, March 2001.
Daigle, L., van Gulik, D., Iannella, R. and P. Faltstrom, "Uniform Resource Names (URN) Namespace Definition Mechanisms", BCP 66, RFC 3406, October 2002.
